summary: This note is a guide by Hartley, Hoover and Salyer on solving real business cycle (RBC) models with a representative agent. It sets up a social planner's problem with technology shocks, derives the equilibrium conditions, and calibrates parameters to postwar U.S. data (alpha=0.36, beta=0.99, delta=0.025, A=3). It then linearizes the system, solves it via eigenvalue decomposition, and simulates artificial series whose volatilities and correlations are compared with U.S. data in Table 1.
one_line: A worked guide to solving and calibrating a real business cycle model with technology shocks, using linearization and eigenvalue methods.
key_facts: The typical real business cycle model assumes an economy of identical infinitely-lived households and firms, reflected in a single representative agent.
Output is produced according to yt = zt f(kt, ht), where zt is the technology shock and the price of output is normalized to one.
The planner's problem uses 0 < beta < 1 as the agents' discount factor and 0 < delta < 1 as the depreciation rate of capital.
The technology shock follows an autoregressive process with autocorrelation parameter 0 <= rho <= 1 and innovation with mean one and standard deviation sigma_e.
Typical calibrated values based on postwar U.S. data (Hansen and Wright, 1992) are alpha = 0.36, beta = 0.99, delta = 0.025, and A = 3.
With these parameters the steady-state values are c = 0.79, k = 10.90, h = 0.29, and y = 1.06.
The calibration implies labor's share of output is 64%, an annual riskless interest rate of 0.04%, a capital-output ratio of roughly 10, and roughly 30% of time spent in work activity.
The Solow residual is detrended linearly over quarterly data for 60.1-94.4, giving an estimated technology shock serial correlation rho of 0.95.
The variance of the technology shock innovation was estimated at 0.007.
The linear system is written as A u_t = B E_t(u_{t+1}), and the stable rational expectations solution is associated with the eigenvalue less than one.
The rational expectations solution includes the restriction c~ = 0.54 h~ ... with c~ = 0.54 h~ + 0.02 k~ + 0.44 z~ in the paper's expression (16) as printed.
Simulated output, consumption and investment were generated from 3000 observations, of which the last 120 were examined.
Table 1 reports that in the RBC model investment has relative volatility 2.86 against 3.02 in U.S. data, with correlation with output 0.95 against 0.80.
The note cites Debreu (1954) for the result that the Pareto optimum matches the competitive equilibrium, and Prescott (1986) for the existence and uniqueness of the solution.
